facts.statement: Bahariasaurus lived during the Cenomanian age of the Late Cretaceous in North Africa.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Bahariasaurus ingens, which was found in North African rock layers dating to the Cenomanian age of the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Bahariasaurus is estimated to have been 11 to 12 meters long and weighed around 4 tons.
facts.quote: Bahariasaurus is among the largest known theropods, estimated at 11 - 12 m long and around 4 t in weight.

facts.statement: Fossils of Bahariasaurus were unearthed in April 1914 at Gebel Ghorabi near Ain Gedid, Egypt, by Richard Markgraf.
facts.quote: In early April 1914, fossils of Bahariasaurus were unearthed from mudstone strata at Gebel Ghorabi near Ain Gedid, Egypt by Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf.

facts.statement: The fossils were transported to Munich in 1922 and formally described by Ernst Stromer in 1934.
facts.quote: It was not until 1922 that they were transported overseas to Munich, where they were described by Stromer in 1934.

facts.statement: The genus name Bahariasaurus combines 'Baharia' (the formation name) and the Latin word 'sauros' meaning lizard.
facts.quote: The generic name Bahariasaurus is combines Baharia, in reference to the Bahariya Formation where the fossils were unearthed, with the Latin root sauros, meaning "lizard"

facts.statement: The species name 'ingens' is derived from the Latin word for 'huge'.
facts.quote: the specific name ingens comes from the Latin word for "huge".

facts.statement: A notable fossil referred to Bahariasaurus is a right femur measuring 1.22 meters in length.
facts.quote: The most notable of these remains was a large, 1.22 m long right femur

facts.statement: Bahariasaurus is estimated to have been 11 to 12.2 meters long and weighed between 4 and 4.6 tons.
facts.quote: Bahariasaurus was a notably large theropod. It may have approached the height and length of other large-bodied theropods such as Tyrannosaurus rex and the contemporaneous Carcharodontosaurus, being estimated as 11 - 12.2 m long and 4 - 4.6 t.

facts.statement: Bahariasaurus is known only from postcranial skeletal material.
facts.quote: Bahariasaurus is only known from postcranial material.

facts.statement: Bahariasaurus has historically been classified within various theropod groups, including Carcharodontosauridae and Tyrannosauroidea.
facts.quote: Historically, the exact taxonomic placement of Bahariasaurus has been uncertain and debated; it has been variously assigned to several theropod groups, including the Carcharodontosauridae and the superfamily Tyrannosauroidea.

facts.statement: The attribution of fossils from Niger to Bahariasaurus is debated, with some researchers suggesting they belong to a carcharodontosaurid while others classify them as Theropoda incertae sedis.
facts.quote: However, the attribution of these fossils to Bahariasaurus is questionable, with some authors stating that they could belong to a carcharodontosaurid whereas Ijouiher (2022) placed it as Theropoda incertae sedis.

facts.statement: In 1996, Paul Sereno and colleagues described a specimen as a new species of theropod named Deltadromeus agilis.
facts.quote: In 1996, the specimen was described by Sereno and colleagues in the journal Science as a new genus and species of coelurosaurian theropod named Deltadromeus agilis.

facts.statement: Ernst Stromer found Bahariasaurus in Africa in 1934 in the Bahariya Formation of Egypt.
facts.quote: Bahariasaurus fue hallado en África en 1934 por Ernst Stromer, en la Formación Baharija de Egipto.

facts.statement: The original fossils of Bahariasaurus were lost during World War II bombings.
facts.quote: Estos restos se perdieron durante los bombardeos de la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

facts.statement: Additional remains of Bahariasaurus were later found in Agadez, Niger.
facts.quote: Luego se encontraron más restos en Agadez, Níger.

facts.statement: Bahariasaurus was a large predator reaching 11 to 12 meters in length and weighing 2.5 tons.
facts.quote: Era un predador de gran tamaño que alcanzó unos 11 a 12 metros de largo y peso 2,5 toneladas.

facts.statement: Bahariasaurus had a more gracile constitution compared to other large theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: pero su constitución era más grácil.

facts.statement: The taxonomic position of Bahariasaurus is uncertain; it was originally classified in Carcharodontosauridae and Tyrannosauroidea, but is now thought to belong in Noasauridae.
facts.quote: La ubicación taxonómica de Bahariasaurus es incierta, originalmente fue clasificado como perteneciente a la familia Carcharodontosauridae y Tyrannosauroidea, aunque ahora se piensa que debe ser incluido dentro de Noasauridae.

facts.statement: There is a hypothesis that Bahariasaurus is simply a juvenile version of Deltadromeus.
facts.quote: Existe también una hipótesis que afirma que este dinosaurio es simplemente una versión juvenil de Deltadromeus.

facts.statement: The fossil record for Bahariasaurus spans from the Albian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 113.2 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Maastrichtian (113.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Bahariasaurus lived in the wetland environment of the Bahariya Formation alongside Tameryraptor and Spinosaurus.
facts.quote: Bahariasaurus is known from the Bahariya Formation, then a wetland environment, alongside the coeval Tameryraptor and Spinosaurus

facts.statement: If Bahariasaurus is an abelisauroid, it may have been related to herbivorous or omnivorous taxa, suggesting minimal competition with carnivorous theropods.
facts.quote: If Bahariasaurus is indeed an abelisauroid, it would have been related to taxa interpreted as being herbivorous or omnivorous, implying minimal resource competition with the coeval carnivorous theropods.
